r: HCPS 2700 prepares students to analyze cannabis-specific health care law: patient-provider-institution relationships, corporate compliance obligations, shareholder responsibility, key controlling cases, and the ongoing federal-state legal conflict that defines this industry. These tasks map onto O*NET activities such as evaluating information for compliance and interpreting legal and regulatory meaning for organizational stakeholders, squarely inside the categories where observed-usage data shows writing and documentation dominate current adoption. Task-exposure research classifies writing as strongly positively associated with exposure, and legal-memo drafting and case synthesis fit that profile. At 24 months, general-purpose AI already drafts compliance summaries and case briefs competently, but this niche's rapid, jurisdiction-specific statutory churn and the absence of a mature specialized tool limit realized deployment. No licensure or accreditation binds this elective, so the near-term constraint is diffusion lag rather than institutional lock-in, yielding a Medium rating.

By 2031, AI legal-research and compliance-drafting tools should routinely handle the survey-level work this course teaches: summarizing statutory and case-law developments, drafting corporate compliance policy language, and comparing state cannabis frameworks against federal prohibition. Observed-usage data already shows enterprise API deployments skewing toward automation rather than augmentation, and five years of further diffusion should push cannabis-adjacent compliance drafting into that automated category as legal-AI products mature and firms adopt them more broadly. Verification burden eases somewhat as citation-checking tooling improves, though jagged-frontier findings caution that misapplied case law outside a model's competence still produces confidently wrong output. No licensure, GT-Pathways designation, or accreditation credit-hour floor protects this elective, and it is not a prerequisite substrate for other required coursework, so nothing structurally caps the rating. The instrumental case for a human performing this survey work is substantially weakened, producing High.

A decade out, capability trends suggest legal-document synthesis, compliance-policy drafting, and case-law comparison across shifting federal-state cannabis frameworks will be routinely delegable, consistent with METR/Epoch findings on the doubling of AI task-time horizons and with programming/writing remaining the most exposed skill categories in task-exposure research. This course's applied output is almost entirely textual analysis rather than embodied or interpersonal judgment, and with no institutional lock-in to hold ground, the rating stays High. The genuine hedge is that cannabis remains an unusually volatile regulatory space; federal rescheduling or new enforcement regimes could generate legal questions novel enough to keep demanding real human legal reasoning rather than pattern-matched precedent, and firm-level AI diffusion, per Census BTOS figures, remains uneven even where capability exists. Ten-year point-prediction confidence is accordingly capped at medium despite the High rating.
HCPS 2700.d: Students in this course will survey the major legal and ethical issues of the health care cannabis systems in the United States. The course covers the legal issues surrounding the relationships of patient, provider, and health care institution as well as historical considerations of cannabis. There will be specific inquiry into how organizations that work with cannabis manage from a legal standpoint. Further, the course will focus on shareholder responsibility, corporate compliance, key cases that control cannabis health care law, federal and state considerations as well as the ongoing changes that are taking place currently. Ethics from the standpoint of the grower, distributor and user will also be considered.

r: HCPS 4000 covers the operational core of running a health care organization: human resources management, finance and budgeting, billing and collections for patient services, risk management, and monitoring operational performance. These map to O*NET activities like staffing organizational units, analyzing data or information, and coordinating work activities — administrative functions with no clinical embodiment or licensure lock. Observed-usage data shows office and administrative work well represented among current AI use, and productivity research on professional writing shows meaningful time savings on report-style deliverables, which fits budgeting narratives and risk memos closely. At 24 months, AI plausibly assists with dashboards and drafting but adoption within health care administration specifically still lags general office use, and the moderate verification burden of getting billing and compliance details right in a regulated setting keeps a human closely involved, yielding Medium.

By 2031, AI should perform much of the analytical and reporting labor underlying health care operations — budget variance analysis, billing and collections dashboards, staffing models, and risk-monitoring reports — consistent with observed enterprise deployments skewing toward automation over augmentation. The applied tasks this course teaches are administrative rather than clinical, carry no accreditation credit-hour floor or licensure mandate, and are not a foundational prerequisite for later required coursework, so no institutional cap holds the rating down. Verification burden remains real in a regulated billing and compliance environment, but oversight increasingly concentrates in narrower judgment calls rather than the broad operational-management competence this course surveys. Productivity research on writing and reporting tasks suggests strong quality and speed gains apply directly to this kind of deliverable. The instrumental case for taking the course to perform these operational tasks is substantially eroded, producing High.

A decade out, health care operations management concentrates around AI-generated dashboards, budgets, staffing models, and compliance reporting, with humans retained mainly for governance and accountability functions that a regulated, litigation-exposed sector still demands. The rating stays High, tracking the exposed administrative and business-knowledge courses rather than the protected clinical ones, because this course's content sits in staffing, finance, and reporting activities the task-exposure literature associates with strong positive exposure. The hedge: health care's heavy regulatory and liability structure could sustain more hands-on operational involvement than a pure capability read implies, macro-level productivity effects from AI diffusion remain modest per TFP estimates, and firm-level adoption unevenness could leave many health systems running these functions largely unchanged. Confidence in the specific ten-year magnitude is accordingly moderate rather than high.
HCPS 4000.d: Students in this course will be introduced to the fundamental elements of operating a health care organization. Basic concepts of human resources management, finance and budgeting, billing and collection for patient care services, risk management, and monitoring of operational performance will be covered in the course.

r: HCPS 4010 teaches students to evaluate evidence-based health care delivery models: appraising research supporting evolving care models, understanding evidence-generating processes, and addressing coordination and knowledge-integration challenges as medical advances accumulate. These map to O*NET activities such as processing information, interpreting the meaning of information for others, and updating and using relevant knowledge — research-synthesis work firmly in the digital, non-clinical category. Task-exposure research finds writing and information-synthesis tasks strongly positively associated with exposure, and observed-usage data shows research and analysis prominent among current deployments. At 24 months AI already summarizes and appraises published literature competently, but the course's applied output feeds delivery-model decisions in a regulated setting, so a meaningful verification burden and still-uneven institutional adoption of AI-assisted evidence synthesis in health administration keep the near-term rating at Medium rather than higher.

By 2031, literature appraisal, synthesis of evidence supporting care-delivery models, and tracking of medical advancements should be routinely AI-assisted, extending the automation-skewed pattern observed in enterprise deployments to this course's core tasks. No licensure gate, accreditation credit-hour floor, or foundational prerequisite role protects the course — unlike its nursing counterpart, evidence appraisal here serves administrative and delivery-model decisions rather than direct bedside application, so the institutional cap that holds down clinical courses does not apply. Verification burden persists where evidence gets misapplied to care-coordination decisions, but that burden narrows relative to the broad synthesis work AI increasingly performs well. Jagged-frontier research is the relevant caution: AI users misapply findings outside a model's competence with misplaced confidence. On balance the instrumental case for taking this course to perform evidence synthesis and appraisal work is substantially weakened, producing High.

A decade out, evidence synthesis and care-delivery-model evaluation are plausibly among the more thoroughly automated activities in the health administration curriculum, since the applied work is almost entirely digital literature and data synthesis rather than embodied or interpersonal practice. Capability-trend evidence on lengthening AI task-time horizons supports continued gains on exactly this kind of multi-step research synthesis. The rating holds at High, consistent with the exposed administrative and evidence-based-practice courses outside licensure programs rather than the protected clinical ones. The genuine hedge: health care delivery decisions carry real consequences, regulatory and liability structures could sustain more human evidence-appraisal involvement than a pure capability projection implies, and diffusion of AI evidence-synthesis tools into health administration programs specifically remains uneven and slower than general-purpose adoption. Ten-year confidence is therefore moderate despite the High rating.
HCPS 4010.d: Students in this course will be introduced to evidence based health care delivery modalities. Students will learn about evolving models of care which incorporate current best practices supported by research and data. Understanding these evidence generating models is essential as the health care industry moves further into the free flow of information and shared knowledge. These health care delivery models are aimed at solving challenges related to coordination of patient care and reducing the time to integrate continuing analysis and synthesis of medical advancements.
